name: Portsmouth
title: Portsmouth Ship Thickness Measurement | Ferry and Ro-Ro UTM
description: Ultrasonic thickness gauging at Portsmouth International Port for ro-pax ferries, cruise ships and cargo vessels: ramps, vehicle decks, tanks and piping.
h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Gauging for Ferries and Cargo Ships in Portsmouth
intro: Portsmouth International Port sends ro-pax ferries to Normandy, Brittany and northern Spain, runs sailings to the Channel Islands, receives cruise ships and works a cargo terminal, all inside a harbour it shares with the Royal Navy's aircraft carriers. The ferries keep tight timetables, but they return to the same linkspans week after week, and that regularity is what makes gauging here practical. For each job a team travels out from India and works on board in the hours the operator can spare between sailings or before a refit.

highlights.p: Ferries on the Normandy, Brittany and Biscay routes often spend a night or a midday gap on the berth. With tanks emptied and ventilated beforehand, the team can gauge ballast tanks, voids and vehicle-deck structure without delaying the next departure.

Ro-ro ships calling several times a week put heavy, repeated loads through stern ramps, bow doors, hinges and the deck around them. UT of ramp plating and MPI of hinge lugs and locking devices show where fatigue and wastage are building up.

Most cross-Channel ferries refit in the quieter months. Readings taken at Portsmouth during the season give the technical department a steel and pipe list to send to the yard, so the refit specification is settled before the ship leaves service.

port.h: Portsmouth: ferry port, naval harbour and Solent gateway
p: Portsmouth Harbour opens to the Solent through a narrow mouth between Old Portsmouth and Gosport, where the tide runs hard and ships pass close enough to the Round Tower for people on the walls to read their names. The harbour is a dockyard port, so movements inside it are controlled by the King's Harbour Master, and warships, Isle of Wight ferries and merchant ships share the same channel under one set of rules. Portsmouth International Port, owned by the city council, lies further up the harbour on Portsea Island, beyond the naval base, with linkspans for the ro-ro ferries, a passenger terminal that also handles cruise ships, and berths for cargo. Larger ships plan their passage through the entrance around the tide and the naval programme.

Brittany Ferries is the largest operator, with ro-pax crossings to Caen, Cherbourg, Le Havre and St Malo and longer sailings across the Bay of Biscay to Santander and Bilbao. Ferries for the Channel Islands also leave from here, and cruise ships call on Channel itineraries or begin their cruises in the city. Wightlink runs car ferries and fast catamarans to the Isle of Wight from Gunwharf, inside the harbour mouth, and the hovercraft crosses to Ryde from Southsea beach. On the cargo side, reefer ships bring in fresh produce and short-sea ships handle general cargo at the port's quays. Behind all of it is the naval base, home to the Royal Navy's two aircraft carriers and much of its surface fleet, which gives the harbour a rhythm of its own.

Inspection demand at Portsmouth follows the ferry calendar. Through the busy season the ships run almost without pause, so gauging is done in short slices: an overnight lay-over, a midday gap, a weekly maintenance window agreed with the operator. In the autumn the emphasis moves to pre-refit scopes, because the winter yard period is short and the yard needs its steel list early. Cruise ships and cargo vessels add occasional work during their calls. Ro-pax structure takes a particular kind of punishment, with vehicles loading over ramps several times a day, vehicle decks flexing under laden trailers and ballast shifted to keep the ship level on the linkspan, and that is where most of the readings end up being taken.

facilities.h: Where ships can be gauged in Portsmouth Harbour and the eastern Solent
p: Most gauging happens at the ferry linkspans and lay-by berths of the international port. A ferry lying overnight gives several hours of steady access: ballast and fresh-water tanks pumped out and ventilated by the crew, voids and cofferdams opened, and vehicle decks clear of traffic so ramps and deck plating can be reached. Work stops when loading begins, so the plan sets out which tanks are done on which visit. Cargo ships at the port's quays are gauged during discharge, with each hold worked as it empties and the hatch covers read while they are open.

The drydocks inside Portsmouth Harbour belong to the naval dockyard, so merchant ships calling here generally go elsewhere for a docking, often to a yard on the Continent or in Spain for the Biscay ferries. That makes Portsmouth a place for in-service and pre-docking gauging rather than for renewal steelwork. Ships waiting to enter can anchor at Spithead or off St Helens on the Isle of Wight, where boarding by launch is possible in settled weather, but a berth is usually only hours away and few owners choose to work at anchor when the quay is so close.
list: Continental ferry linkspans — vehicle-deck, ramp and hinge inspection on ro-pax ferries between sailings, timed around loading.
Lay-by and overnight berths at the international port — staged ballast tank and void gauging over consecutive visits ahead of a winter refit.
Passenger terminal berth — piping, tank and exterior structure readings on cruise ships during a day call.
Cargo quays — hold, hatch-cover and tank-top readings on reefer and general cargo ships as cargo comes out.
Gunwharf and the Isle of Wight ferry berths — shell, deck and piping checks on car ferries and fast craft during maintenance periods.
Spithead and St Helens anchorages — launch-borne deck and air-pipe readings on ships held outside the harbour.

context.h: Port state control, emissions rules and ferry regulation at Portsmouth
p: Foreign-flagged ships calling at Portsmouth are inspected by the Maritime and Coastguard Agency, which applies Paris MoU procedures under UK law. For the ferries, a larger regulatory driver is the EU's climate package: voyages between Portsmouth and French or Spanish ports bring half their emissions under the EU Emissions Trading System and half their energy use under FuelEU Maritime, for ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above. Operators have answered with newer LNG-fuelled and hybrid ships alongside older tonnage fitted with scrubbers, and each brings its own inspection points, from fuel-tank cofferdams to wash-water lines.

Ro-pax ships also live with closer scrutiny of their watertight and weathertight integrity than most cargo ships, because of stability lessons the industry learned the hard way on open vehicle decks. Bow doors, inner ramps, stern doors and their securing arrangements are examined by class, flag and the operator's own superintendents, and wastage or cracking around them is treated seriously. Gauging that tracks plate thickness at ramp hinges, door frames and the vehicle-deck plating nearest the ramps gives the operator evidence to plan renewals rather than react to a surveyor's finding.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs in Portsmouth
jobs.p: Portsmouth jobs are planned with the ferry operator's technical department, and the scope is cut to fit the time each ship spends alongside. Larger programmes are spread across several calls so that no sailing is delayed, with the same technicians returning each time and the readings tied to one set of frame references. Cruise and cargo ships are handled call by call, with the agent confirming the berth and the hours available. The aim on every job is the same: readings the superintendent can use to decide what to renew, when, and at which yard. These are the jobs we most often plan around this port's timetable.
list: Pre-refit steel estimate on a Biscay ro-pax: ballast tanks, voids and vehicle-deck plating gauged across several overnight lay-overs during the autumn.
Stern ramp, bow door and hinge inspection on a cross-Channel ferry, with UT of ramp plating and MPI on hinge lugs and cleats, done in a midday gap.
Scrubber wash-water and overboard pipe UT on an older ferry before its refit, so replacement spools can be made ahead of the yard period.
Hold and hatch-cover gauging on a reefer or general cargo ship discharging at the port's cargo quays.
Piping and tank readings on a cruise ship during a day call, in an order the chief engineer sets before arrival.
Condition gauging of an Isle of Wight car ferry ahead of its annual maintenance period.

logistics: Heathrow and Gatwick are the usual arrival airports, with trains from London to Portsmouth Harbour station or a drive down the A3; Southampton Airport is closer but has fewer international connections. The international port, the naval-controlled harbour and the ferry berths are all secured areas, so the ship's agent or the operator's port team arranges passes against each technician's passport before the visit. Technicians from India need a UK visa, so we fix the lay-overs we will use well in advance and keep the dates agreed with the operator.

faqs.q: Can a ferry be gauged during an overnight lay-over at Portsmouth?
faqs.a: Yes. A ferry lying overnight at the international port gives several hours of steady access once the last vehicles are off. The crew empty and ventilate the tanks on the agreed list before arrival, the team gauges them in priority order, and work finishes before loading starts. On a full pre-refit scope we spread the tanks over several lay-overs so nothing holds up a sailing.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock in Portsmouth for merchant ships?
faqs.a: The drydocks in Portsmouth Harbour serve the naval dockyard, so merchant ships calling here normally dock elsewhere. What Portsmouth offers instead is regular, predictable time alongside, which suits building a pre-docking steel estimate. The readings go to whichever yard the ship is booked into, on the class formats and with sketches, so the yard can plan the steelwork before the ship arrives.

faqs.q: Do you inspect stern ramps, bow doors and vehicle decks on ro-pax ships?
faqs.a: Yes. These are the areas that take the most repeated loading on a ferry. We measure plate thickness on ramps, door frames and the deck plating around them, and use magnetic particle testing on hinge lugs, cleats and welded brackets where fatigue cracks start. Findings are reported to the superintendent on the day, referenced to the ship's frame numbers.

faqs.q: Can ships be gauged at anchor at Spithead?
faqs.a: It is possible by launch, booked through the agent, when the weather allows safe boarding and the harbour authorities agree. In practice most ships waiting off Portsmouth enter within hours, so we usually wait for the berth, where tanks can be opened and gas-free certification is simpler to arrange. Anchorage time is worth using only for deck, air-pipe and hatch readings that need no tank entry.
